q: Fossil Xinicaulis trees widened their trunks in a startling way. What happened to the network of woody strands inside them as they grew?
d: These ancient trees had many interconnected woody strands around a hollow center. Fossils indicate controlled splitting and collapse helped accommodate an expanding trunk.
s: Chinese Academy of Sciences · Fossil tree growth
choices: It was replaced by an expanding pith
It was shed outward as successive bark layers
It fused into one solid central cylinder
evidence: Research institution’s account of2017 PNAS study explicitly describes hollow cylindrical woody skeleton tearing and collapsing as diameter expanded.

q: Roots release strigolactone signals that help establish partnerships with fungi. Which unwelcome neighbors can exploit those same signals to start growing?
d: Witchweed and broomrape seeds use these root chemicals as clues that a potential host is nearby. A helpful invitation to fungi can also announce a meal to a parasite.
s: Annals of Botany · Strigolactone signaling review
evidence: Author review covers strigolactones as AM-fungus recognition signals and Striga/Orobanche germination stimulants. PMC direct view CAPTCHA; indexed text and PubMed abstract read.

q: Research on wild yeasts found some heritable traits carried by changes in what, without a corresponding change in DNA sequence?
d: Self-propagating shapes of prion proteins can pass a cellular trait onward. In the studied yeasts, some such traits were beneficial under particular environmental conditions.
s: Nature · Prion inheritance in wild yeasts
evidence: Primary survey of wild Saccharomyces finds self-templating prion conformations and conditionally beneficial heritable phenotypes; no claim all prions are beneficial.

q: Chemical analysis of cicadas infected with Massospora fungi uncovered which surprising class of compounds?
d: Researchers detected cathinone in infected periodical cicadas and psilocybin in certain infected annual cicadas. Detection alone did not establish exactly how those chemicals affect the insects’ behavior.
s: Fungal Ecology · Alkaloids in cicada pathogens
evidence: Primary metabolomics identifies cathinone and psilocybin in different cicada–Massospora pairs; avoids asserting drug-driven behavioral mechanism.

q: The South African rat’s-tail plant grows a tall, bare stalk that carries no flowers. What useful service does this stalk provide?
d: A sunbird sitting on the stalk reaches down to the ground-level flowers. Its posture places its body where pollen can be transferred efficiently.
s: Nature · Specialized bird perch in Babiana
choices: A storage organ for dry-season water
evidence: Primary Babiana ringens study identifies sterile inflorescence axis functioning exclusively as bird perch and positioning malachite sunbirds for cross-pollination.

q: The orchid Acampe rigida flowers when insect visits are scarce. What can physically move its pollen into its own stigma?
d: Splashes remove an anther cap and flick the pollen masses upward. A connecting strap pulls them back into the flower’s receptive cavity, providing self-pollination during wet weather.
s: Annals of Botany · Rain pollination in Acampe
evidence: Primary observations and rain-shelter experiments describe drop-driven cap removal, pollen ejection and elastic return to stigma; no autonomous self-pollination without rain.

q: Without a visiting insect, the orchid Holcoglossum amesianum can pollinate itself through which unusual movement?
a: Its anther rotates into its own stigma
d: The pollen-bearing structure turns through a full circle against gravity and inserts pollen into the receptive cavity. The flower performs the transfer itself.
s: Nature · Self-pollination in Holcoglossum
choices: Its anther rotates into its own stigma
Its petals shake pollen into a central cup
Its stigma folds upward around the anther
Its entire flower turns upside down
evidence: Primary abstract describes anther turning360degrees against gravity into own stigmatic cavity, with no agent or medium.

q: A 2016 study found an additional fungal resident embedded in the outer layer of many lichens. What was this overlooked resident?
d: The researchers found basidiomycete yeasts alongside the familiar main fungus and photosynthetic partner. Lichen communities can be more complex than a simple partnership of two organisms.
s: Science · Additional yeast partners in lichens
evidence: Primary paper abstract at University of Glasgow repository reports specific basidiomycete yeasts in cortex across many lichens; no assertion all lichens require this third partner.

q: A crypt-keeper wasp develops inside another wasp living in an oak gall. What temporary exit plug does the parasite eventually chew through?
d: The infected host drills an undersized exit and dies with its head blocking it. The developing parasite later escapes through that head, using an opening its host prepared.
s: Proceedings of the Royal Society B · Crypt-keeper wasp manipulation
choices: A cap of hardened plant resin
A ball of chewed leaf fibers
evidence: Primary Bassettia pallida/Euderus set study documents manipulated emergence drilling, head plugging and parasite escape; plant-gall ecological interaction.

q: Some acacias make their protective ants more dependent on them by interfering with which ability of the ants?
d: A protein in the plant’s nectar inhibits the ants’ sucrose-splitting enzyme. The ants then rely on the host’s nectar, in which that sugar has already been broken down.
s: Ecology Letters · Nectar-mediated partner dependence
evidence: Primary paper reports nectar chitinase inhibits Pseudomyrmex gut invertase after workers’ first nectar meal; dependence on sucrose-free host nectar.

q: Some Macaranga trees protect their resident ants with a barrier that excludes many other climbing insects. What forms this barrier?
d: The plant’s specialized ant partners can run over the waxy stems, while many competitors and predators cannot. The surface acts as a selective climbing barrier.
s: Oecologia · Macaranga wax barriers
evidence: Primary study and Cambridge biomechanics research account describe epicuticular wax blooms excluding generalists while symbiotic ants climb effectively.

q: Ants living inside the hollow leaves of Dischidia major supply more than discarded food. Which gas from the colony can the plant recycle?
d: Isotope analysis linked a substantial share of the occupied leaves’ carbon to respiration associated with the ants. The leaf chambers provide a local carbon source as well as shelter.
s: Nature · Ant-derived carbon in Dischidia
evidence: Primary stable-isotope study estimates39percent leaf carbon from ant-related respiration; no precision required in card.

q: Inside some swollen ant-plants, smooth chambers serve as nurseries while warty chambers receive rubbish. What useful job do the warty surfaces perform?
d: Ants leave food remains and other debris against the absorptive surfaces. The plant’s internal architecture separates brood rooms from sites that help feed its host tissues.
s: National University of Singapore · Rubiaceous ant-plants
choices: Cooling the chambers by evaporating water
Sealing discarded material away from living tissue
evidence: Museum botanical account contrasts smooth chambers with highly absorptive lenticel-like warts at waste deposits; lowland Hydnophytum not generalized to all chambers.

q: What cue can Cayratia tendrils use when deciding whether to curl around another plant’s leaf?
d: The tendrils avoid oxalates concentrated in their species’ leaves. They also avoided oxalate-coated plastic sticks, supporting chemical detection through contact.
s: Proceedings of the Royal Society B · Tendril contact chemistry
choices: The direction of the leaf’s shadow
evidence: Primary experiments show avoidance of oxalate-coated sticks and correlation with leaf oxalate content; contact chemoreception supported, not consciousness.

q: Which parts of a bumblebee can act as tiny moving sensors of a flower’s weak electric field?
d: The field deflects fine hairs, producing neural activity. This gives the bee an additional source of floral information beyond color and scent.
s: PNAS · Bumblebee mechanosensory hairs
evidence: Primary study measures electromechanical hair deflection and corresponding neural activity; related commentary distinguished hairs from antennae.

q: A 2023 study challenged the usual explanation for the crystal-like bladder cells on quinoa and common ice plant. What major function did the experiments reveal?
d: The cells formed chemical and physical barriers against arthropod attackers. In the tested plants, their role in salt and drought tolerance was much smaller than had long been assumed.
s: Current Biology · Epidermal bladder cell defenses
evidence: Primary2023 study reports minor/absent abiotic protection and chemical/physical herbivore barrier; explicitly framed as study-specific revision, not broad universal rejection.

q: Which feature of sea rocket fruit helps some seeds travel while others stay close to the parent?
a: A detachable upper segment and retained lower segment
d: The upper segment travels more readily, while the retained lower portion favors offspring close to the parent. A single fruit supports contrasting dispersal strategies.
s: Brazilian Journal of Botany · Cakile fruit dispersal
choices: Two halves that burst open in opposite directions
A detachable upper segment and retained lower segment
An edible outer layer surrounding a sticky inner seed
A floating outer seed surrounding a sinking inner seed
evidence: Primary Cakile maritima study: distinct upper/lower segments, upper dispersal versus seedlings near parent chiefly from lower segments; Bath thesis corroborates retention. Existing11813 only identifies species.

q: In a laboratory evolution study, some populations of single-celled green algae gained protection from predators by evolving what arrangement?
d: After repeated exposure to a filter-feeding predator, some Chlamydomonas populations evolved multicellular forms. Survival tests found that those traits helped resist being eaten.
s: Scientific Reports · Predation and multicellularity
evidence: Primary2019 experiment: two of five selected populations evolved multicellularity; assays supported protection. Not all populations and not instantaneous transformation.

q: In experiments on yellow Lantana flowers, what tiny event was enough to trigger a color change?
a: A pollen grain landing on the stigma
d: Pollination could initiate the change even with a single grain. A pollen extract also triggered it, suggesting that a chemical factor in pollen supplied the signal.
s: Journal of Experimental Botany · Lantana flower color
choices: A petal being touched by a leg
A grain of sand landing on an anther
A drop of nectar being removed
A pollen grain landing on the stigma
evidence: Primary1984 experiment reports even one pollen grain sufficient and pollen extract mimicking effect. No unsupported claim all color change requires pollination.

q: Male and female shoots of one studied moss attract tiny animal visitors with different versions of what signal?
d: Ceratodon moss emits sex-specific volatile mixtures. The attracted microarthropods can assist sperm transfer, creating a pollination-like partnership in a plant without flowers.
s: Nature · Sex-specific moss scents
evidence: Primary Ceratodon purpureus study measures sex-specific volatile cues, differential microarthropod attraction and improved fertilization; terrestrial scent system distinct from algal waterborne sperm transport.

q: Roridula traps insects on sticky leaves but lacks the usual means to digest them itself. Which partners help it obtain nutrients from the catch?
d: Pameridea bugs eat the trapped insects and deposit nutrient-bearing waste on the leaves. The plant can benefit from prey that its resident insects process.
s: Oecologia · Roridula digestive mutualism
evidence: Primary Roridula dentata/Pameridea paper identifies obligate digestive mutualism and lack of digestive enzymes; foliar absorption supported independently by PMID15728666.

q: Male Welwitschia cones contain a sterile ovule-like structure. Instead of producing a seed, what does it offer insect visitors?
d: The modified reproductive structure secretes a sweet reward. Even the male cones retain this female-like feature as part of the plant’s pollination system.
s: Kirstenbosch · Cultivation of Welwitschia
evidence: Kirstenbosch author describes sterile modified pistil-like structure exuding nectar. SANBI indexed page corroborates; SANBI direct HTTP403 and later PDF find timed out after successful open.

q: The orchid Epipactis veratrifolia tricks female hoverflies into laying eggs on its flowers. What larval food does it falsely advertise?
d: The orchid imitates aphid colors and alarm scents, attracting mothers seeking prey for their larvae. Investigating flies transfer pollen but leave eggs without the expected food supply.
s: BMC Evolutionary Biology · Aphid mimicry in an orchid
evidence: Primary2014 report says aphid coloring and alarm pheromone mimicry induces hoverfly oviposition on false brood sites. Target false nursery distinct from attacked-bee smell luring adult food thieves.

q: In very dense experimental rows, neighboring sunflowers improved their access to light by arranging their stems into what pattern?
d: Adjacent plants leaned toward opposite sides of the row. Local responses to the light environment produced a coordinated pattern without a central organizer.
s: PNAS · Self-organization of sunflower stands
choices: A shared lean in one direction
An arch with only the end plants upright
A spiral around the row’s center
evidence: Primary field study shows alternating stem inclinations propagating along high-density rows via red/far-red responses; distinct from daily tracking and mature heads facing east.

q: Laser scans of silver birches in calm weather revealed what subtle overnight change in their branches?
d: Branches and foliage shifted downward during the night, then returned toward their starting positions in the morning. The observations measured movement, without establishing human-like sleep.
s: TU Wien · Overnight movement of birch trees
choices: They rose and remained raised through the morning
They spread outward and stayed extended
They twisted steadily around the trunk
evidence: First-party research account describes two birches, calm conditions without condensation, gradual night drooping and morning return; internal clock versus sunlight unresolved.
